runs.text: Cordão da Catana tecido, & feitotodo redõdo.

lines.note: Continues the Maruuchi example from f307: the sword cord is woven and made entirely round. Catana is a Japanese sword term inside the Portuguese explanation; the close printed feitotodo is retained.
Maruyama is a rounded hill or mountain. The scan begins an independent headword flush with the other entries, not an indented continuation.
Maruzaya is a rounded scabbard. It is another independent entry; the provisional indentation is removed to match the left edge in the scan.
Maſa and maſame describe a way of sawing boards. The Portuguese manner of cutting is explained below, and maneira remains divided at manei-.

runs.text: ra q̃ não pareção as veas: comũmente são de hũ

lines.note: The boards are sawn so that the grain or veins do not show in the stated way; they are commonly of a specified wood. The scan restores são from OCR ão while preserving comũmente and hũ.
The wood is compared to cypress, with the historical acipreſte retained. Vide introduces the upright Japanese cross-reference Itame, not a new headword on this row.
Maſacari is an axe. The short entry is flush left in the scan and is not subordinate to the preceding timber definition.
Maſago is sand from the shore. The printed Area da praya is retained without adding modern accents or changing the historical spelling.

Maſame cross-refers to Maſà and Itame. Both referenced Japanese forms are upright; the scan supports the period after Maſà and retains its apparent grave rather than copying the OCR's partial italicization.
Maſana and maſanano describe something not upright, sound, or legitimate. The negative definition continues across the division of recta.
Ta completes recta, followed by the qualities sound and legitimate. Maſanano begins a Japanese example applying the adjective to a person.

runs.text: Homẽ não recto, ou que não he ſolido.

lines.note: Fito completes Maſanano fito, an unsound or dishonest person. The Portuguese Homẽ retains its nasal abbreviation and directly explains the example.
Maſani is an adverb meaning soundly or rightly. The final S. is visibly upright and marks written usage; it is not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Maſaqino cazzura is a climbing plant used on a trellis or arbour. The comparison with ivy continues below; the scan does not justify a more specific botanical identification.
Mo completes como era, like ivy. This short Portuguese continuation explains the plant's climbing habit and closes the entry.
Maſari means surpassing or exceeding. Iz- begins the Japanese example, whose negative contrast says that none was better or worse.
Completes Izzuremo maſari, votoriua nai, with neither superiority nor inferiority among them. The Portuguese translation begins Todos e- and continues below.
Completes erão iguais, they were equal. Taif. is an upright citation label; Lib. 29. is italic, and the visible final period is restored from the scan.
The nominal Maſari denotes advantage or excess. Keep it separate from the preceding verb and retain the printed double-s sort in exceßo.
Maſſauo is glossed here as being completely green. The example starts Iro in continuous upright type; the OCR's isolated italic r is removed without modernizing the colour term.
Iro maſſauoni natta describes the colour becoming wholly green. The Portuguese Acor is closely set as printed, and totalmente is divided at total-.
Mente verde completes the colour description. The dictionary's green gloss is preserved even though modern Japanese colour associations might suggest a different translation.
Maſaxij means upright, true, or faithful. The final adjective fiel is physically divided after fi-.
El completes fiel. Maſaxij fito applies the adjective to an upright and faithful person; the example remains separate from the derived forms that follow.
Maſaxiſa is the nominal form, uprightness or truthfulness, associated with Maſaxij. It is a complete short physical row and needs no invented Portuguese gloss.
Maſaxǔ and maſaxiqu are alternative adverbial forms. Preserve the caron on u and the printed alternative marker l rather than normalizing the morphology.
Maſotto means a little more. The source has a single s-type here, unlike the doubled consonants in the neighbouring emphatic headwords.
Maſſacari is the prime, bloom, or vigour of an age or condition. The example below applies it to flowers in full bloom.
Fanano maſsacari introduces the time of full flowering. The mixed long-and-round s pair in this occurrence is retained rather than made identical to the headword above.

runs.text: das as roſas, ou fulas florecem.

lines.note: Das completes todas: all the roses or flowers are blooming. The historical word fulas is preserved as printed, not silently replaced with flores.
Maſſacaſama means completely reversed or upside down. The scan supports a in ſama, correcting OCR ſuma without altering the printed doubled s-types.

Maſsacaſamani is the corresponding adverbial form. The Portuguese visibly repeats the as sequence in às asaueßas; preserve this printed anomaly rather than silently correcting it to ordinary às aueſſas.
The sense is head downward. The example begins Maſſacaſamani, using the printed s-types of this occurrence independently of the preceding headword.

runs.text: Cair com a cabeça pera baixo.

lines.note: Votçuru completes the example of falling headfirst. Initial v represents the historical spelling of the Japanese verb and is not replaced by modern o.
Maſſacaſamano describes something entirely contrary or reversed. The scan reads às, not OCR ds; the following example applies the term to an accusation.
Maſſacaſamano vttayede atta describes an accusation that was completely the reverse of the truth. Foi begins its Portuguese translation, continued below.

runs.text: acuſação totalmente ao contrario do que paſou.

lines.note: The accusation was wholly contrary to what happened. Retain paſou with one s-type: its o is worn and open-looking, but the image does not warrant an invented second s or a normalized spelling.

runs.text: Meo, vigor, ou força da couſa.

lines.note: Maſsaichǔ denotes the middle, full vigour, or height of something. The mixed long-and-round s pair is read locally, not made uniform with adjacent occurrences.

The Japanese example describes passing along the shore during the battle of the Genji and Heike. The third glyph of Iſcuo is c-like in the scan; retain that apparent printed form rather than silently regularizing it to the expected Iſouo. Final maſ continues on the next physical line without a printed hyphen.

The continuation completes the expression for the battle being at its height. A visible two-armed mark supports ǔ rather than OCR ù in ſaichǔde. Yax. is an upright citation label; Portuguese pra continues below as praya without a printed hyphen.

runs.text: ya era conjunção em que o Feique, & Guenji

lines.note: Ya completes praya, and the Portuguese says that the Heike and Genji were then engaged in battle. Feique and Guenji are Japanese names embedded in the printed italic explanation, not separate headwords.

runs.text: eſtauão no meo, ou fragrante da batalha.

lines.note: The battle was at its height. Preserve printed fragrante rather than silently substituting the expected flagrante; the unusual wording does not justify changing the visible type.

Restore the visible paragraph sign before the example meaning the heart of winter. The worn final accent in maſſaichù does not securely show both arms of a caron, so retain the supplied grave reading here rather than copying the clearer mark from another occurrence.
Do Inuerno completes the preceding explanation, the middle or heart of winter. It is an indented continuation, not a new entry.
Maſſaqi means the very front. The example Maſſaqini ſu- begins taking the lead, with the printed hyphen retained at the physical line ending.
The first example is completed and a second begins, Maſſaqi uo caquru, to go in front. The capital is visibly M, correcting OCR Naſſaqi; this line is indented like the other continuations.

The gloss says to go in the vanguard. The final Japanese word has capital Q, not G: Qimi begins an example addressed to one's lord, continued at the top of column 2. Preserve the printed word separation nadianteira.

This continues Qimi from the foot of column 1: going before one's lord and undertaking to die fighting. The final tçucamatçurǒ- retains its visible diacritic and line-end hyphen; no new entry starts here.

runs.text: Indo na dianteira, ou diante de

lines.note: Zu completes the Japanese future form. Yax. is the upright source label, followed by the Portuguese translation about going in the vanguard before one's lord.

runs.text: meu ſenhor ei de morrer pelejando.

lines.note: The scan reads ei, not ci, in the historical spelling of the Portuguese future expression ei de morrer, 'I shall die.' This completes the previous column's example and remains indented.
Maſsǒ is an adverbial affirmation, 'that is so; you are right.' It begins a flush-left entry; preserve the locally printed long-and-round s pair.
Maſſoba means very close. The example visibly has two long s-types, Maſſobani iru, correcting the omitted s in the draft. This is a flush-left headword, not an indented continuation.
The Portuguese translates the preceding Japanese as being very close to someone. The historical joined form dalguem is retained.

Maſsono introduces expressions for being at the very edge or immediately nearby. The printed headword and the example have different s-type combinations; retain them independently. Final bor- continues into bordinha below.
Dinha completes bordinha. A paragraph sign introduces further Japanese examples, Maſſono ſoba and maſsono atari; these are standalone examples rather than terms embedded in Portuguese.
The Portuguese explains the examples as being right there, very near or adjacent. This is an indented continuation of Maſsono.
Maſſore, maſsore is a repeated affirmation, rendered 'that is so, that is so.' Preserve the distinct printed s-types rather than harmonizing both occurrences; the entry is flush left.
Maſsuguna describes something very straight or upright. Its nominal/adjectival ending belongs to the headword, and the full line begins at the headword margin.
Maſu denotes the measure used for rice, wheat, and similar goods. The Japanese measure word is a headword here, not an embedded typeface-toggle term.
This second Maſu is a river fish, distinct from the measure in the preceding entry. Its independent headword begins at the left text margin.
Maſugata is illustrated by Faxirano maſugata, the capital of a column. Retain the Japanese example in roman type and the printed split Ca-/pitel.
Pitel completes Capitel da columna, the architectural capital. This short line is an indented continuation, not another headword.
Maſu maſu means increasingly, or more and more. The repeated Japanese form and the Portuguese progression 'once, and again more, and...' continue into the next line.

Mais completes the gloss of Maſu maſu. At the far right of this same sloping row the scan prints a parenthesis-like mark and limpo, completing the following entry's 'clear and clean' gloss. Preserve these displaced elements here, not in semantic reading order. The draft's c2-l018 was an overlapping duplicate OCR detection, not another physical body row.

Maſumino cagami is a poetic expression for a clear, clean mirror. The italic P. introduces the explanation; limpo is printed at the far right of the preceding physical row and is represented there. The headword occurs only once in the scan.

Maſurauo is marked as poetic and equated here with a mountain hunter. The scan shows a circumflex in reôxi, not a caron. P. is upright in this occurrence, unlike the slanted P. in the preceding explanation; the Japanese synonym after i, is not an embedded Portuguese term.
Do mato, ou caçador completes the definition as a man of the wilds, or hunter. Preserve the Portuguese formulation without adding a broader modern definition of Maſurauo.
Adverbial Mata means again, another time. It is a separate entry from the homonymous anatomical or branching term below.

runs.text: Abertura como dantre os dedos, ou das

lines.note: The second Mata denotes an opening or division, like that between fingers or legs. The historical contraction dantre is retained.

The example Te axino mata refers to the spaces associated with hands and feet. Abertura begins the Portuguese explanation continued below; retain the printed terminal stop even though the sentence continues.

runs.text: dantre os dedos das mãos, & dos pees.

lines.note: The explanation specifies the gaps between fingers and toes. The printed tildes in mãos and the historical spelling pees are preserved without modernization.
Matabiquan denotes a servant of another servant, a subordinate retainer. The q and the full final quan are supported by the headword's visible letters.

runs.text: Hum pao como forcado com q̃ me-

lines.note: Mataburi is a forked wooden implement. The gloss begins explaining that salt makers use it to put fuel into the furnace; me- is a physical word division continued below.

runs.text: tem lenha no forno os que fazem ſal, &c.

lines.note: Tem completes metem. The rest explains the use of this fork for placing firewood in a salt-making furnace; the final &c. belongs to that definition.
Matagari gives the verb for standing with the legs or feet spread. Retain the supplied st representation in Estar rather than undertaking a global ligature recoding.
The example begins Monni mataga-, standing astride or across the gate. The scan has t in mataga-, correcting OCR macaga-; the printed hyphen continues the Japanese verb below.

runs.text: Porſe à porta com os pees largos, & fei

lines.note: Ru completes matagaru. The Portuguese describes standing at the doorway with feet wide apart and in a manner meant to block entry; final fei continues into feição without a visible hyphen.

runs.text: ção de não deixar entrar a ninguem.

lines.note: Ção completes feição, and the explanation specifies not letting anyone enter. The indented line belongs to the preceding doorway example.
Matague, uru, eta gives a verb for spreading or extending the legs or feet. Preserve the entry's inflectional endings and the distinction from Matagari.
Axiuo mataguete a- begins the example of walking with the legs spread or with long strides. The printed hyphen divides the Japanese ayumu across physical lines.
Yumu completes ayumu, translated as going with long steps. This short line completes the preceding example and remains indented.
Matagura denotes the division or root of the legs, the crotch. The historical Portuguese arreigada is retained; the following compounds extend the branching sense.
Futamata is a fork with two points. The paragraph sign places this as an example under the branching definition, rather than a new flush-left entry.
Mitçumata is a fork with three points. Preserve the tç spelling and its position as the second indented example.
Matagui is a forked piece of wood. Its final gui is distinct from the qi spelling in nearby unrelated entries and is supported by the scan.
Matai describes someone candid, simple, and upright. The moral sense belongs to this adjective rather than to the preceding forked-wood vocabulary.
Mata itoco denotes second cousins. Preserve the visibly separated Japanese words instead of joining them into a modern compound spelling.

runs.text: O tornar a dormir outra vez.

lines.note: Matane, marked with an upright poetic-register P., means going back to sleep. The P. stands separately from the italic Portuguese explanation in the scan.
Matano toxi is equated with Nochino toxi, the following year. The synonym after i, remains ordinary Japanese reference text, and an- continues into anno below.
No completes anno, and the gloss clarifies 'the year that comes.' This is an indented continuation rather than a separate flush-left line.

runs.text: Hũa fruita de hũa certa era que ſerue

lines.note: Matatabi is described as a fruit of a certain climbing plant. Preserve the printed era and historical fruita rather than substituting a modern botanical name.
De mezinha completes the statement that the fruit serves as a remedy. The short line is indented as part of the preceding definition.
Matataqi is explained through opening and closing the eye. The following paragraph gives the brief interval associated with a blink.

The example means the interval of a blink. The scan reads quanto, with a visible t omitted by the OCR. Preserve the tilde in abrẽ and the comma at the page ending; the bottom catchword & anticipates the continuation rather than belonging to this body row.
